body.text: Sharjeel Imam, an Indian Muslim student activist who has been in jail since 2020 on charges relating to his alleged role in instigating communal riots in Delhi that year, recently gave an interview to The Quint news outlet.

Imam’s interview has sparked much debate in India, particularly because it presents a vision of India that is starkly at odds with the project of the modern Indian state and its constitution. Whatever one may think about the circumstances of his arrest — he has been both denied bail and trial — his ideas on India’s constitutional and political arrangement are problematic and deserving of criticism.

At the heart of Imam’s vision is the need for the Muslim community to have “community rights.” Community rights refer to group or corporate rights, which is the notion that groups can have certain rights particular to their group rather than those possessed by society — and all the individuals belonging to it — at large. This idea is necessary, as per Imam, because Muslims are a separate nation apart from, and distinct from, the larger mass of Indians, who are majority Hindu. Imam’s preference is for a “constitutional arrangement in which Muslims will have full autonomy to administer their affairs, carry out those reform programs, etc without fear of violence and interference from the majority community.”

The reason given for this proposal is the assertion that Muslims have faced discrimination within the modern Indian state, something that is true in some times and places. But his definition of discrimination goes beyond combating bigotry and guaranteeing constitutional rights so every citizen of India is treated with equal dignity. Rather, he alleges Muslims are discriminated against by the very circumstance of living under a constitution “which gave no statutory guarantees to Muslims.”

As the pseudonymous Muslim writer Ibn Khaldun Bharati noted in ThePrint news portal, Imam essentially rejects the framework of liberalism, rather than criticizing the Indian state for not living up to liberalism. According to Ibn Khaldun, Imam “dismisses liberalism as a ploy for majoritarianism… he contemptuously rejects any suggestion of a difference between liberals and Hindutvadis. For him, both are simply Hindus. In his essentialist worldview, all Hindus are the same, for they are unanimous in denying Muslims the political power they claim as a divine right….” In other words, the liberal promise of constitutionally protected individual rights is problematic by its very nature in denying groups their corporate rights. It privileges the group — and its desire to preserve its own distinctive traditions, laws, and customs — over the larger body of citizens which form the Indian nation.

Imam’s arguments are not new, nor are they exclusive to him or his community. In fact, India has long had a problem of groups demanding group rights, quotas on the basis of caste and gender, disproportionate regional representation, and various other schemes to privilege the rights of communities at the expense of individuals. In each instance, despite very different historical justifications, the logic is similar: a belief that a community’s needs or importance entitle it to a special dispensation, reserved seats, or legal privileges.

On the subject of needs, one of Imam’s defenders, Asim Ali, notes in The Telegraph that Imam’s proposals lie within the tradition of radical democratic politics, arguing that communities should organize around their own particular demands before negotiating with other communities. Imam holds that various underprivileged communities like Muslims and Dalits must work together and fight for decentralization, autonomous institutions, and proportional representation, making it more difficult for the majority to exercise power over minorities.

At the heart of this issue is a question: should India’s constitutional model be that of a country of individual citizens and individual rights or a country of corporate communities, including various religious groups, regional ethnicities, and jatis (castes)?

As Muslim leaders gathered at Simla in 1906 suggested to the British Viceroy of India, Lord Minto, “any kind of representation, direct or indirect, and in all other ways affecting their status and influence, should be commensurate not merely with the numerical strength but also with their political importance.” Subsequently, separate electorates were established for the Muslims of British India. A separate electorate is different from a quota or reserved seat in that only members of a specific group, who have their own voter roll, can elect their own representatives.

This led to demands for separate electorates for other groups, such as Dalits (formerly “Untouchables”). Negotiations between Indian independence leader Mohandas K. Gandhi and Dalit leader Bhimrao R. Ambedkar led to the Poona Pact in 1932, in which Dalits gave up their demand for a separate electorate but retained seats reserved for members of their community that the entire electorate could vote for. This compromise is enshrined in India’s post-independence constitution, which adopted the classical liberal propositions of one man, one vote, and a single electorate undivided by caste or religion (Article 325), while also making an allowance for some reserved seats.

The demand for group rights, laws specific to certain groups, quotas, and reservations, though rooted in a desire to remedy past injustices, has morphed into ways for groups to acquire privileges and entrench their power. They are not about protecting the constitutionally guaranteed rights of Indian citizens — only strict adherence to the constitution’s guarantee of individual equality under the law would accomplish that.

Entrenching more group rights would help permanently institutionalize the division of Indian society — already an issue — into a large number of groups with different privileges. It would also help justify majoritarianism as well, because if minorities have group rights, why not the majority?

Ultimately, this line of thinking could inhibit the true emergence of a modern state and society because it keeps a large number of people trapped in zero-sum, communal competition. For, if one group can have certain special rights in how they manage their personal relations, why not another group? If one group has its own electorate or a certain quota, why not another group — that would seem fair, after all. One group securing favorable representation is another group’s loss because it decreases the latter group’s percentage of representation.

Sharjeel Imam’s interview engendered debate because his ideas are so combustible. By seeking to define the Indian Muslim community as a distinct nation, by seeing oppression in the denial of specific group rights, and by alleging that India’s modern nation-building project is illegitimate and fake — an oppressive construct rather than an attempt to build a nation-state that guarantees all its citizens equal rights as individuals — he lays the groundwork for his solution: the fragmentation of the Indian social body itself. This would potentially lead to the Balkanization of citizenship and endless internecine domestic conflict. His logic points to a state seen not as one body of equal citizens, but as a negotiated compact among separate communities. It is hardly a formula for a functioning nation-state.

The alternative is a polity guided by an electorate that at least can aspire to vote on the basis of seeking solutions to economic, developmental, and national security issues, the very issues that a strong, modern nation-state is constituted to handle. This is, after all, the raison d’être of nation-building. In the 1940s, a key philosophical difference between the Indian National Congress (INC) and the All-India Muslim League was between their visions. The INC sought a stronger, more centralized government inhabited by a diverse but undivided Indian nation. But the Muslim League saw India as a land inhabited by separate nations, which necessitated proportional representation, devolution, and eventually, partition. In an era characterized by swift technological change, economic challenges, and geopolitical threats, India seems wise to have gone down the path that it did, not a path similar to the one Sharjeel Imam is advocating.
